Studies and policy changes to pre-incision administration demonstrated significant decreases in post-cesarean infections , and a meta-analysis showed no clear evidence of harm to the child from brief exposure at birth .
Either practice is acceptable and more effective than placebo .

The WHO guidelines recommend a single dose  after  the cord is clamped and cut due to concerns regarding neonatal antibiotic exposure and sepsis .

per_sentence.text: Strong guideline recommendation:  Guidelines state to administer appropriate parenteral prophylactic antimicrobial agents  before skin incision  in all cesarean section procedures ( Category IA–strong recommendation; high-quality evidence ) .
When given, antibiotics should be administered within  1 hour (60 minutes) prior to incision   (or completed within 1 hour of incision if vancomycin is used ).

Efficacy & safety before incision:  Administering prophylactic antibiotics during the hour before incision is likely more effective at reducing post-cesarean infections (such as surgical site infection and endometritis) than waiting until the cord is clamped, and meta-analyses show no clear evidence of harm to the newborn from brief exposure at birth .

Alternative/historical practices:  In the past, concern regarding neonatal antibiotic exposure led some guidelines (such as the WHO  Managing complications in pregnancy and childbirth ) and protocols to recommend delaying administration until immediately after the umbilical cord is clamped and cut .
While either practice is more effective than placebo , current high-quality evidence and recommendations favor administration before skin incision .

rows.question: If my post-op patient is short of breath and we suspect a PE, do we need a chest X-ray before booking her for a V/Q scan or CTPA, and what's the radiation risk to the baby?

A normal CXR prior to V/Q scanning improves the likelihood of obtaining a definitive V/Q result .
If the CXR is  normal , a V/Q scan is typically performed .
If the CXR is  abnormal  and clinical suspicion of PE remains, a  CTPA should be performed in preference to a V/Q scan  .
The radiation dose to the fetus at any stage of pregnancy is negligible (less than 0.01 mSv) .

The International Commission on Radiological Protection estimates an increased risk of fatal childhood cancer up to age 15 of  0.006% per mGy  (or  1 in 17,000 per mGy ) following  in utero  radiation exposure .

rows.question: If my post-op patient is short of breath and we suspect a PE, do we need a chest X-ray before booking her for a V/Q scan or CTPA, and what's the radiation risk to the baby?

per_sentence.text: A CXR should be performed before deciding upon further diagnostic tests, as a normal CXR prior to V/Q scanning improves the likelihood of a definitive V/Q result.
When the chest X-ray is abnormal and there is a clinical suspicion of PE, CTPA should be performed in preference to a V/Q scan.
The radiation dose to the fetus from a CXR performed at any stage of pregnancy is negligible (less than 0.01 mSv).

CTPA is more readily available,37,38 delivers a low radiation dose to the fetus (see section below) and can identify other pathology including pneumonia (5–7%), pulmonary oedema (2–6%) and rarely aortic dissection.5,35 Despite these potential advantages of CTPA, many authorities continue to recommend V/Q scanning as first-line investigation in pregnancy because of its high negative predictive value in this situation and its substantially lower radiation dose to pregnant breast tissue (see section below).39,40 Clinicians arranging imaging scans for suspected PE in pregnancy should be aware of the potential risks surrounding fetal and maternal radiation exposure.41 CTPA exposes the fetus to similar or lower amounts of radiation as V/Q scanning, although studies have been confounded by the type and model of scanners used, the imaging protocols employed and the methods used to estimate radiation exposure.42 With both techniques, the doses employed are well below accepted thresholds for teratogenicity, fetal death and fetal growth restriction, and the main concern for the fetus is a very small increased risk of childhood cancer.43 The International Commission on Radiological Protection has estimated an increased risk of fatal childhood cancer to the age of 15 following in utero radiation exposure of 0.006% per mGy, which equates to a risk of 1 in 17 000 per mGy.44 The fetal radiation exposure associated with CTPA and V/Q is approximately 0.1 mGy and 0.5 mGy respectively, although quoted figures vary considerably.25,43,45 While CTPA is associated with a low risk of radiation for the fetus, this must be offset by the relatively high radiation dose (up to 20 mGy) to the mother’s breast tissue, which is associated with an increased risk of breast cancer.

rows.question: Our ergometrine vials have been sitting in the theatre drug cupboard at room temperature — is that okay to give for PPH prevention, or do we need to switch to something else?

per_sentence.text: World Health Organization (WHO):  Ergometrine is a heat-sensitive drug.

rows.question: My post-op patient is septic and her chart says 'penicillin allergy' — how do I know if that rules out cephalosporins or carbapenems, and what can we give instead?

per_sentence.text: WHO and RCOG:  Cephalosporins and carbapenems (e.g., ceftriaxone, imipenem) can trigger anaphylaxis and are  contraindicated  in patients with a history of penicillin anaphylaxis or severe beta-lactam allergy.
In general, WHO notes that antibiotics are contraindicated in patients with prior immediate/anaphylactic reactions to that specific agent.
RCOG:  Cephalosporins are noted as acceptable substitutes in certain  non-severe  beta-lactam-allergic contexts.
CDC:  Cephalosporins may be contraindicated depending on the nature of the allergy; cross-reactivity and tolerance must be screened before defaulting to a cephalosporin substitute.
WHO & RCOG:  Recommend a combination of  clindamycin plus gentamicin .
RCOG:  Recommends  vancomycin  as an option in severe penicillin allergy, and advises adding vancomycin to clindamycin/gentamicin if MRSA is suspected.
WHO & CDC:   Vancomycin, clindamycin, or teicoplanin  can replace beta-lactams for known or suspected staphylococcal infections or Gram-positive coverage.
RCOG:  Notes clindamycin as an alternative in beta-lactam-allergic patients, but warns of rising resistance.
NICE & RCOG:  High-risk sepsis mandates rapid broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour.

(Note: RCOG's general empirical regimen for life-threatening puerperal sepsis includes clindamycin combined with meropenem or piperacillin/tazobactam, provided carbapenems/penicillins are not contraindicated by severe allergy).
OpenRN:  Blood cultures should be drawn prior to starting antibiotics, with regimens tailored later based on susceptibility testing.

NICE and RCOG  agree on the standard of administering IV antibiotics within 1 hour for high-risk sepsis.
